01.actor: A student of Rabbi Eliezer who was liable to death by burning
01.event: A student of Rabbi Eliezer was liable for burning for his sins against God, and the Rabbis said to leave him alone.
01.turn: Because he had served a great person, the Rabbis chose not to punish him.
01.outcome: He was let off; the passage does not say what the sin was or narrate anything further.
01.summary: A student of Rabbi Eliezer had incurred the penalty of death by burning for a sin against God. The Rabbis said to leave him alone, because he had served a great man. That is all the text tells; the sin and the aftermath are not given.
01.missing: What the student did, who the great person was, and any further events.

02.actor: Rabbi Helbo, Rabbi Avira and Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina, then Rabbi Elazar
02.event: Three sages visiting a place were served a peach as large as a stewpot and shared it out; the next year Rabbi Elazar was served a peach so small he held it in one hand.
02.turn: The fruit had shrunk dramatically from one year to the next.
02.outcome: Rabbi Elazar quoted a verse that a fruitful land becomes a salt waste because of the wickedness of its inhabitants.
02.summary: Three rabbis arrived at a certain place and were served a peach as big as a five-se'a stewpot. They ate a third, declared a third ownerless, and fed a third to their animals. A year later Rabbi Elazar came there and was served a peach he could hold in one hand, and he said that the land had turned barren because of its inhabitants' sins.

03.missing: The passage is a Gemara question about an earlier statement by Rabba bar Avuh; he proposes to give his daughter to Rav Nahman if his flesh steams, but no event, turn or outcome is told.

04.actor: A son sent by his father to fetch chicks from a rooftop nest
04.event: At his father's command a man climbed to the roof, sent away the mother bird and took the young, fulfilling two commandments.
04.turn: On his way back he fell and died, despite the promise of long life attached to those commandments.
04.outcome: The reward was explained as belonging to the world that is entirely good and long, the World to Come. (The passage itself, segments 4 to 6, only debates the incident.)
04.summary: A father told his son to climb to the roof and bring him chicks. The son sent away the mother bird and took the young, thereby keeping two commandments that promise long life. On the way down he fell and died, and the sages read the promised reward as meant for the World to Come.
04.missing: The shown PASSAGE (segments 4 to 6) is only later questioning of this incident; the narrative itself is in context segment 3, and the ladder detail is in segment 7.

05.actor: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin
05.event: They bought a maidservant to be paid in perutot, gave a silver piece as collateral instead of the money, and the price of the maidservant later rose.
05.turn: The sale was disputed when the price rose.
05.outcome: Rabbi Ami ruled that there were no perutot and no valid silver payment, so no acquisition had occurred.
05.summary: The sons of Rav Huna bar Avin bought a maidservant for copper coins they did not have, and gave a piece of silver as collateral. When her price went up, they came before Rabbi Ami. He ruled that no valid payment had been made, so the purchase was not complete.

06.missing: The passage is a legal argument: Rava challenges Rav Nahman with a baraita and Rav Nahman stays silent, which the Gemara then discusses. There is no event to retell.

07.actor: A man who came before Rabbi Ami and the man he claimed was a priest
07.event: A man told Rabbi Ami that another had established presumptive priesthood, citing that he was called first to read the Torah.
07.turn: Rabbi Ami probed whether the first reading was due to priesthood or greatness, and learned a Levite read after him.
07.outcome: Rabbi Ami raised the man to the priesthood on the basis of that statement. (The passage itself, segments 4 and 5, is only a quoted debate.)
07.summary: A man came to Rabbi Ami claiming another man was presumptively a priest because he had read the Torah first in the synagogue. Rabbi Ami asked whether that was because he was a priest or just a great man, and the man said a Levite had read after him. On that basis Rabbi Ami accepted him as a priest.
07.missing: The shown PASSAGE (segments 4 and 5) is Rav Huna's reported argument about halla; the narrative is in context segment 8.

08.actor: A man who rented out a millstone and the man who rented it
08.event: The owner rented a millstone in exchange for grinding, later grew rich and bought another millstone and a donkey, and then demanded money rent.
08.turn: The owner no longer needed the grinding service and asked for payment instead.
08.outcome: The renter refused, offering only to grind; the passage does not state a ruling.
08.summary: One man rented a millstone to another in return for grinding. He later became rich, bought his own millstone and a donkey, and told the renter to pay money since he no longer needed grinding. The renter answered that he would grind as agreed but had not agreed to pay money.
08.missing: How the dispute was resolved; the passage only states the competing claims.

09.event: As he was dying, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi named Babylonian places and their sins, including a town whose people trapped fish on Shabbat, were excommunicated and apostatized.
09.turn: He announced that on that day Adda bar Ahava had entered the covenant and Rav Yehuda was born.
09.outcome: He died, and the Gemara draws the lesson that a righteous person is born as another dies.
09.summary: On his deathbed Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi spoke about various places in Babylonia, describing the lineage flaws of some and a town whose people netted fish on Shabbat and, after being excommunicated, left Judaism. He then said that Adda bar Ahava was being circumcised that day and Rav Yehuda was born. It is a deathbed speech more than a developed story.
09.missing: The passage is a list of pronouncements rather than a sequence of events; the births and ending are in segment 5.

10.event: Rav Hamnuna sat studying before Ulla, who praised him but regretted that his city was Harpanya, whose people are of flawed lineage.
10.turn: Rav Hamnuna was ashamed, and Ulla asked where he paid his poll tax.
10.outcome: Rav Hamnuna said Pum Nahara, so Ulla concluded he belonged to Pum Nahara and his lineage was not flawed.
10.summary: Rav Hamnuna was studying before Ulla, who exclaimed that he would be a great man were it not for his hometown Harpanya, a place of impaired lineage. Rav Hamnuna was ashamed. Ulla asked where he paid his poll tax; it was Pum Nahara, so Ulla said he was really from there and his lineage was fine.

11.event: Acher saw the tongue of Hutzpit the interpreter being dragged along the street by a pig after Hutzpit's execution.
11.turn: He asked whether a mouth that produced pearls should lap up dirt.
11.outcome: He left the faith and sinned.
11.summary: According to one account, Acher saw the tongue of the executed Hutzpit dragged through the street by a pig. He cried out that a mouth that had produced pearls should not lick dust. That sight led him to go out and sin.

12.event: A widow's son asked Rabbi Eliezer whom to honor first when both parents ask for water, and then asked Rabbi Yehoshua.
12.turn: When he asked what if his mother were divorced, Rabbi Yehoshua replied sarcastically that his tears showed he was a widow's son.
12.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua told him to pour water for them and call them like chickens, meaning neither takes precedence.
12.summary: A widow's son asked Rabbi Eliezer which parent to serve first when both ask for water, and was told to set aside his mother's honor for his father's. Rabbi Yehoshua gave the same answer. When the man asked what if the mother were divorced, Rabbi Yehoshua said it was clear he was a widow's son and sarcastically told him to pour water for both.

13.actor: Ameimar, Mar Ukva and other judges
13.event: Several judges accepted a small favor from a stranger, such as removing a feather or covering spittle.
13.turn: The stranger then said he had a case to bring before them.
13.outcome: Each judge disqualified himself from hearing the man's case.
13.summary: While Ameimar was judging, a feather landed on his head and a man removed it, then said he had a case before him; Ameimar said he was disqualified. Similarly, a man covered spittle lying before Mar Ukva and was told by Mar Ukva that he could not judge his case.

14.event: Rav and Rav Yehuda were walking on a road with a woman walking ahead of them.
14.turn: Rav told Rav Yehuda to lift his feet away from Gehenna, and Rav Yehuda objected that Rav had permitted such seclusion for men of good character.
14.outcome: Rav explained that he meant men like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and his colleagues, not ordinary scholars like themselves.
14.summary: Rav and Rav Yehuda were traveling when a woman walked ahead of them. Rav urged Rav Yehuda to hurry away from such danger, and Rav Yehuda reminded him he had permitted this for the upright. Rav replied that the upright meant people like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi, not the two of them.

15.actor: Hama, son of Rabba bar Abbahu, acting for Avimi
15.event: Avimi sent money via Hama to pay a debt in Bei Hozai, and Hama paid and asked for the document back.
15.turn: The creditors said the money was for side debts and refused to return the document; Hama had no witnesses of the payment.
15.outcome: Rabbi Abbahu ruled that since they could have denied the payment entirely, they could also claim it was for side debts, so Hama could not recover money or the document.
15.summary: Avimi sent money through Hama to repay creditors, and Hama paid them and asked for the document. They said the payment went to other debts and kept the document. Hama came before Rabbi Abbahu, admitted he had no witnesses, and was told that they could just as well have denied the payment, so their claim stood.

16.actor: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai and Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter
16.event: Riding out of Jerusalem, Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai saw a young woman gathering barley from animal dung, who covered herself with her hair and asked him for sustenance.
16.turn: She revealed she was the daughter of Nakdimon ben Guryon, and reminded him he had signed her marriage contract promising a huge dowry.
16.outcome: Rabban Yohanan wept and said that when Israel does not do God's will, they are delivered even to the animals of a lowly nation.
16.summary: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai, leaving Jerusalem with his students, saw a young woman picking barley from animal dung. She asked for his support, said she was Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter, and recalled that he had signed her marriage contract for a vast dowry. He told his students he remembered, and wept over how far she had fallen.

17.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya
17.event: When Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi fell ill, Rabbi Hiyya visited and found him crying.
17.turn: Rabbi Hiyya asked why he cried, citing a baraita that dying while crying is a bad sign.
17.outcome: Rabbi said he was crying for the Torah and the commandments he would no longer be able to fulfil.
17.summary: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi was ill, and Rabbi Hiyya came to him and found him in tears. Rabbi Hiyya asked why he cried, reminding him that dying in tears is a bad omen. Rabbi answered that he wept for the Torah and mitzvot he would no longer be able to perform.

18.actor: The wife of Rav Yosef, son of Rav Menashya of D'vil
18.event: She came before Rav Yosef to claim support from her late husband's estate, asking for sustenance, wine, and then silk garments.
18.turn: When asked why she needed silk, she answered it was for him, his friends and his friends' friends, so as not to be ashamed in front of them.
18.outcome: Not stated whether the silk was granted; sustenance and wine were granted.
18.summary: A widow came before Rav Yosef and asked for sustenance, which he apportioned, and then wine, which he also apportioned. She then asked for silk garments, and when he asked why, she said it was so she would not be ashamed before him and his colleagues.
18.missing: Whether Rav Yosef granted the silk.

19.event: He left for the study hall without waiting for Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai, stayed twelve years, and returned to find the paths of his city changed.
19.turn: He followed a girl called daughter of Hakhinai, whom he realized was his own daughter, to his house, where his wife saw him and died of shock.
19.outcome: He prayed that God have mercy on her, and she was revived.
19.summary: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai went to study for twelve years and came back to a city whose paths had changed so that he could not find his house. He heard a girl being called daughter of Hakhinai, guessed she was his daughter, and followed her home. His wife saw him and her heart gave out, but he prayed for her and she lived.

20.missing: Rabbi Zakkai teaches a baraita and Rabbi Yohanan tells him to go teach it outside; this is a brief exchange about a legal ruling, with no developed narrative.
